Serving as Ukraine's Minister of Defence from late 2021 until his dismissal in 2023, this politician previously held several other senior government roles in Kyiv — who is he?

This historical region of northeastern Greater Iran became the political and cultural base of the Parni people and the Arsacid dynasty — lending its name to a famous empire. Which region?

Parthia: Historical region located in northeastern Iran. Parthia (Old Persian: 𐎱𐎼𐎰𐎺 Parθava; Parthian: 𐭐𐭓𐭕𐭅 Parθaw; Middle Persian: 𐭯𐭫𐭮𐭥𐭡𐭥 Pahlaw) is a historical region located in northeastern Greater Iran.

Its name comes from Ancient Greek for "love of wisdom," and once upon a time physics and psychology were considered branches of it before going their separate academic ways. What rational, critical field is this?
Philosophy: Study of general and fundamental questions.
Often depicted as a beautiful woman with butterfly wings, this mortal-turned-immortal endured trials set by Venus to win back her husband Cupid in Apuleius's The Golden Ass — who is she?
Psyche (mythology): Wife of Cupid. Psyche is known from the ancient Roman proto-novel The Golden Ass (also known as the Metamorphoses), written by philosopher and orator Apuleius in the 2nd century.
Trained as a lawyer, this conservative French statesman served three stints as prime minister before becoming president in 1913 — who is he?
Raymond Poincaré: President of France from 1913 to 1920.

Of Jewish descent, this Czechoslovak-born media baron escaped the Nazis, won a British Army decoration, served as a Labour MP, and built an empire that swallowed the Mirror Group and Macmillan — who was he?
Born in London to a Pakistani family, this Labour politician served as MP for Tooting before becoming the third mayor of London in 2016?
Sadiq Khan: Mayor of London since 2016. Sir Sadiq Aman Khan (born 8 October 1970) is a British politician serving as the third and current strategic authority mayor for London since 2016.
Before becoming Australia's 30th prime minister in 2018, this politician ran Tourism Australia and served as the New South Wales Liberal Party's state director — who is he?
Scott Morrison: Prime Minister of Australia from 2018 to 2022.
Known by the honorific Bangabandhu, this founding president of Bangladesh was assassinated in a 1975 coup after leading the country since 1972 — who is he?
Sheikh Mujibur Rahman: Bangladeshi revolutionary and statesman (1920–1975)
After finding fame as Tulsi in India's most-watched soap opera, this actress-turned-politician joined the Bharatiya Janata Party in 2003 and later held roles in India's Union Cabinet — who is she?
Smriti Irani: Indian actress and politician (born 1976)

This East African Muslim state, ruled by a hereditary sultan from 1856 to 1964, once controlled a coastal strip of Kenya before losing it and eventually being overthrown by revolutionaries — what was it called?
Sultanate of Zanzibar: 1856–1964 East African Muslim state. It was also involved in the shortest war in history, the Anglo-Zanzibar War, which lasted 38 minutes on the morning of 27 August 1896.
Convicted for conspiring in the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing, this Michigan-born man briefly served in the U.S. Army alongside his co-conspirator before their plot together — who is he?
The military government of Japan from 1603 to 1868, established after the Battle of Sekigahara and based in Edo Castle—what is this shogunate called?
Tokugawa shogunate: 1603–1868 Japanese military government (Edo Jidai)

Exemplified by thinkers like Saint-Simon, Fourier, and Robert Owen, this early-19th-century current imagined ideal, non-capitalist societies but was later dismissed by Marxists as impractical — what is it called?
Utopian socialism: Political theory concerned with imagined socialist societies.
This Ukrainian-born Russian military blogger and convicted bank robber, who became a pro-war propagandist, was assassinated in a Saint Petersburg bombing in April 2023 — who was he?

Vladlen Tatarsky: Russian military blogger (1982–2023). Tatarsky was active as a propagandist for Russia and the separatist forces in Ukraine until he was assassinated in a bombing in Saint Petersburg in April 2023.

After nine years as a CIA clandestine officer, this politician represented a sprawling 550-mile Texas border district in Congress before mounting a brief 2024 presidential bid and endorsing Nikki Haley — who is he?
Founded by Grigory Yavlinsky and translating to 'Apple' in Russian, this social-liberal party held seats in the State Duma before losing its faction status in 2003 — which party?
Yabloko: Russian political party. The party consequently participated in the elections of deputies of the State Duma of the Federal Assembly of the Russian Federation of all eight convocations.
Mentioned in the Book of Exodus as the wife of Moses and daughter of the Midianite priest Jethro, this woman was the mother of Moses' two sons — who is she?
Which of these four is the eldest?
Patrick Geddes (born 1854) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these people was born first?
Omar Khayyam (born 1048) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four has been around longest?
C++ (founded 1983) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the oldest?
Haskell (founded 1990) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the astronomer from these four.
Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin is an astronomer. Despite completing her studies, because she was a woman Payne was not eligible to receive a degree from the University of Cambridge.
Who among these is a mathematician?
John Horton Conway is a mathematician. John Horton Conway (26 December 1937 – 11 April 2020) was an English mathematician.
What is the atomic number of Plutonium?
Plutonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Pu and atomic number 94.
What is the atomic number of Rhenium?
Rhenium is a chemical element; it has symbol Re and atomic number 75.
In what year was Jane Goodall born?
Jane Goodall: Dame Valerie Jane Morris Goodall ( GUUD-awl; née Morris-Goodall; 3 April 1934 – 1 October 2025) was an English primatologist and anthropologist.
In what year was Jan Hus born?
Jan Hus: Hus is considered to be the first Church reformer, even though some designate the theorist John Wycliffe.
In what year was Enrico Fermi born?
Enrico Fermi: With his colleagues, Fermi filed several patents related to the use of nuclear power, all of which were taken over by the US government.
In what year did Galileo Galilei die?
Galileo Galilei: Galileo has been called the father of observational astronomy, modern-era classical physics, the scientific method, and modern science.
In what year did Paracelsus die?
Paracelsus also had a substantial influence as a prophet or diviner, his "Prognostications" being studied by Rosicrucians in the 17th century.
In what year was Tardigrade discovered?
Tardigrade: The earliest known fossil is from the Cambrian, some 500 million years ago.
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-17: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. The MiG-17 was license-built in China as the Shenyang J-5 and Poland as the PZL-Mielec Lim-6.
NASA X-43: Boeing. The NASA X-43 was an experimental unmanned hypersonic aircraft with multiple planned scale variations meant to test various aspects of hypersonic flight.
Cannoli: Italy. Cannoli are Sicilian pastries consisting of a tube-shaped shell of fried pastry dough, filled with a sweet and creamy filling containing ricotta cheese.
Who is credited with discovering Copernicium?
GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
Copernicium: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research. Copernicium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cn and atomic number 112.
Who is credited with discovering Pluto?
Pluto: Clyde Tombaugh. Pluto (minor-planet number 134340) is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, a ring of bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Who is credited with discovering Influenza A virus?
Influenza A virus: Christopher Andrewes. Influenza A virus, or IAV, is a pathogen with strains that cause seasonal flu in humans; it can also infect birds and some mammals.
First flown in 1987, this medium-lift helicopter began as a joint UK-Italian venture between Westland and Agusta, and several countries use the nickname 'Merlin' for it — which helicopter is it?
AgustaWestland AW101 is a medium-lift helicopter in military and civil use.
In 1978, a run-in with a particle accelerator's proton beam left this Russian physicist with an extraordinary survival story after it passed straight through his head — who is he?
Anatoli Bugorski (born 25 June 1942) is a Russian retired particle physicist.

Once classified as bacteria and originally called archaebacteria, this domain of mostly single-celled prokaryotic organisms turns out to be the ancestral lineage from which eukaryotes evolved — which domain of life?
Archaea (ar-KEE-) is a domain of organisms.
One of the first grains ever domesticated, this cereal crop was cultivated in the Fertile Crescent around 9000 BC and later spread throughout Eurasia by 2000 BC — name the grain?
Barley (Hordeum vulgare), a member of the grass family, is a major cereal grain grown in temperate climates globally.
Represented most commonly as a 1 or a 0, this portmanteau of 'binary digit' is the most fundamental unit of information in computing — what is it called?
Bit is the most basic unit of information in computing and digital communication.
This cabbage-family vegetable, whose large dark-green flowering head is eaten as food, closely resembles its paler relative cauliflower — name it?
Domesticated roughly 6,000 years ago in Mexico, this nightshade produces berries in red, green, and yellow ranging from mild to fiery — what is its scientific name?
Capsicum annuum is a flowering plant in the family Solanaceae (nightshades), native to the northern regions of South America and to southwestern North America.
Its other name is varicella, it spreads through the air, and it tends to hit adults harder than children — which itchy, blister-forming disease is this?
Chickenpox is a highly contagious disease caused by varicella zoster virus (VZV), a member of the herpesvirus family.

Lacking the sucking mouthparts of aphids, this chewing-mouthed insect is considered one of the most primitive alive — and a famous few of its 4,600 species became notorious household pests. What is it?
Cockroach (or roaches) are insects belonging to the order Blattodea (Blattaria).
Which compound acts as a cellular buffer and, via its phosphorylated form, hands phosphate groups back to ADP to recharge ATP in muscle and brain?
Creatine (or) is an organic compound that, in vertebrates, facilitates recycling of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), primarily in muscle and brain tissue.
Defined as having at least three loose or watery bowel movements in a day, this common condition can quickly cause dehydration, especially in children. What condition is it?
Diarrhea (American English), also spelled diarrhoea (British English), is the condition of having at least three loose, liquid, or watery bowel movements in a day.
Trained in both mathematics and philosophy, which Austrian-German thinker developed the concept of phenomenological reduction and founded a major 20th-century school of philosophy?
Edmund Husserl (Austrian; 8 April 1859 - 27 April 1938) was an Austrian-German philosopher and mathematician who established the school of phenomenology.

Discovered in January 2005 by a Palomar Observatory team and named after a Greco-Roman goddess of strife, this trans-Neptunian object is the most massive known dwarf planet in the solar system — which one?
Eris (dwarf planet) (minor-planet number 136199) is the most massive and second-largest known dwarf planet in the Solar System.
Bred in Brazil as a guard dog, cattle herder, and big-game hunter, this large mastiff-type breed was also once used to catch runaway slaves — which breed?
Fila Brasileiro (Portuguese) is a Brazilian breed of large working dog of mastiff type.
Sometimes mistakenly called the 'stomach flu' even though it's unrelated to influenza, this inflammation of the gut is usually viral, with rotavirus the top cause in children. What condition is it?
Gastroenteritis is an inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract including the stomach and intestine.
Defined as one joule of absorbed radiation energy per kilogram of matter, this SI measure is used in radiotherapy dosing and predicting acute radiation sickness — which measure is this?
Gray (unit) (symbol: Gy) is the unit of ionizing radiation dose in the International System of Units (SI), defined as the absorption of one joule of radiation energy per kilogram of matter.
Classified as acute if it resolves within six months and chronic if it persists longer, this inflammation of the liver can progress to cirrhosis or liver cancer — which condition?
Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver tissue. Acute hepatitis can resolve on its own, progress to chronic hepatitis, or (rarely) result in acute liver failure.

In this heart condition, muscle tissue — most often in the wall between the ventricles — thickens for no obvious reason, weakening the heart's pumping and sometimes its electrical rhythm — name the condition?
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM, or HOCM when obstructive) is a condition in which muscle tissues of the heart become thickened without an obvious cause.

A colorless, flammable organic compound with a pungent odor, this liquid is miscible in water, ethanol, and chloroform, and is widely used as a solvent and disinfectant. It's commonly abbreviated as IPA—what is it?
Isopropyl alcohol (IUPAC name propan-2-ol and also called isopropanol or 2-propanol, commonly abbreviated as IPA) is a colorless, flammable, organic compound with a pungent odor.
Famed first for studying diamagnetism, which Irish physicist proved in 1859 the link between atmospheric CO2 and what we now call the greenhouse effect?
John Tyndall (2 August 1820 - 4 December 1893) was an Irish physicist.

Named after a French mathematician but reportedly learned from his Swiss tutor, this calculus theorem evaluates tricky limits by taking derivatives of the numerator and denominator — what is it called?
L'Hôpital's rule (loh-pee-TAHL) is a mathematical theorem used for evaluating the limit of a quotient of two functions, each of which tends to zero or infinity, by taking each function's derivative.
Popular in aquariums but a destructive invader in the Atlantic and Mediterranean, this venomous Indo-Pacific creature warns predators off with bold red and black stripes — what is it?
Lionfish (genus Pterois) are venomous marine fish native to the Indo-Pacific.
Domesticated in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago from wild teosinte, this grain was grown by Native Americans alongside beans and squash in the 'Three Sisters' method — name the tall grass crop?
Maize (Zea mays), also known as corn, is a tall stout grass that produces cereal grain.
Shaped like a half-moon, this crescent of fibrocartilage partly divides the knee joint and also turns up in the wrist, jaw, and shoulder joints — what is it called?
Meniscus (anatomy) (pl.: menisci or meniscuses) is a crescent-shaped fibrocartilaginous anatomical structure that, in contrast to an articular disc, only partly divides a joint cavity.
These cylindrical, burrowing insects have small eyes and shovel-like front limbs highly adapted for digging underground — name the family?
Mole cricket are members of the insect family Gryllotalpidae, in the order Orthoptera (grasshoppers, locusts, and crickets).
In this category of over 80 recognized conditions, the body's adaptive immune system mistakenly attacks its own healthy tissue as though it were foreign. What is it?

Navel (clinically known as the umbilicus; pl.: umbilici or umbilicuses; also known as the belly button or tummy button) is a protruding, flat, or hollowed area on the abdomen at the attachment site of the umbilical cord.
This massive bony fish, weighing up to a metric ton, resembles a giant fish head without a tail and is native to tropical and temperate waters worldwide. What is it?
Ocean sunfish (Mola mola), also known as the common mola, is one of the largest bony fish in the world.
Pair it with aspirin and caffeine and it's a first-line remedy for mild headaches; on its own it's the active ingredient many people know as acetaminophen — what is this over-the-counter drug?
Paracetamol is an analgesic and antipyretic agent used to treat fever and mild to moderate pain.
This flowering plant genus's name traces to a Tupi-Guarani word for tobacco, borrowed via French — which South American garden favorite is it?
Petunia is a genus of 20 species of flowering plants of South American origin.
Emerging roughly 203 million years ago and wiped out alongside the dinosaurs 66 million years ago, this order of long-necked marine reptiles ruled Jurassic seas — what were they?
Plesiosaur are an order or clade of extinct Mesozoic marine reptiles, belonging to the Sauropterygia.

Found below the bladder with the urethra passing through it, this male reproductive gland acts as a mechanical switch between urination and ejaculation, and produces fluid that becomes part of semen — name the gland?
Prostate is an accessory gland of the male reproductive system and a muscle-driven mechanical switch between urination and ejaculation.
This transhumanist inventor who pioneered text-to-speech and OCR technology later won the $500,000 Lemelson-MIT Prize in 2001 for his work on artificial intelligence — who is he?
Ray Kurzweil (born February 12, 1948) is an American computer scientist, author, entrepreneur, futurist, and inventor.
Born in 1858, this German inventor devised a compression-ignition engine so significant that it and its fuel now both carry his surname — who was he?
Rudolf Diesel (18 March 1858 - 29 September 1913) was a German inventor and mechanical engineer.
As chief technology officer of a Turkish defense company, this engineer designed Turkey's first indigenous combat drone and its first unmanned fighter jet — who is he?
Selçuk Bayraktar (born 7 October 1979) is a Turkish pilot, engineer and businessman.
With the formula Na2CO3, this odorless white salt yields an alkaline solution in water and earned the name 'soda ash' because plant ashes once gave it up. What is it?
Sodium carbonate (also known as washing soda, soda ash, sal soda, and soda crystals) is the inorganic compound with the formula Na2CO3 and its various hydrates.
Lacking the powder down that herons and ibises use to clean off fish slime, these bill-clattering wading birds come in 20 living species across six genera — which birds?
Stork are large, long-legged, long-necked wading birds with long, stout bills.
This protective cap of repetitive nucleotide sequences guards the ends of eukaryotic chromosomes from progressive degradation — what is it called?
Telomere (from Ancient Greek (tlos) 'end' and (mros) 'part') is a region of repetitive nucleotide sequences associated with specialized proteins at the ends of linear chromosomes (see Sequences).
A nasty complication of this inflamed-throat illness goes by the wonderfully old-fashioned name 'quinsy,' or peritonsillar abscess — what's the underlying condition?
Tonsillitis is inflammation of the tonsils in the upper part of the throat.

First identified in 1801 by a Spanish-Mexican scientist analyzing a mineral he dubbed 'brown lead,' this hard, silvery-grey transition metal carries atomic number 23 and chemical symbol V — what's the element?
Vanadium is a chemical element; it has symbol V and atomic number 23.
Caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene, this inherited condition lets copper build up in the liver and brain, leading to tremors, personality changes, and yellowing skin — which condition?
Wilson's disease (also called hepatolenticular degeneration) is a genetic disorder characterized by the excess build-up of copper in the body.
This painful collection of pus built up within body tissue often causes redness, warmth, and swelling, and includes boils and carbuncles as common types — what is it called?
Abscess: Localized collection of pus in body tissue. An abscess is a collection of pus that has built up within the tissue of the body, usually caused by bacterial infection.
This wide-body twinjet shares its wing and much of its structure with the four-engined A340, and it first carried passengers for Air Inter in January 1994 — which aircraft is it?
Native to Europe, Western Asia, and North Africa, this flowering plant lent its name — and originally its root — to a fluffy campfire treat, and is used in herbal medicine — which plant?

Affecting about 1 in 15,000 people, this rare genetic disorder causes severe intellectual disability, little to no speech, and balance problems — yet those affected are often noted for a notably happy personality. Which condition is it?
Angelman syndrome: Genetic disorder caused by a mutation of chromosome 15.
Also nicknamed the cross spider or diadem spider for the white markings on its back, this orb-weaver is native to Europe but was introduced to North America — what species is it?

Araneus diadematus: Species of spider. The spider species Araneus diadematus is commonly called the European garden spider, cross orbweaver, diadem spider, orangie, cross spider, and crowned orb weaver.

Steel-blue with wavy black markings on its back and silvery underneath, this shoaling fish thrives in the cooler waters of the Mediterranean, Black Sea, and northern ocean near Europe — which species?
Atlantic mackerel: Species of fish. The Atlantic mackerel's body is elongate, steel-blue marked with wavy black lines dorsally and silvery-white ventrally, its snout long and pointed.

Members of the family Ursidae walk flat on plantigrade paws tipped with five claws that can't retract — and though most eat meat, the giant panda among them is mostly herbivorous. What animal is this?
Colloquially called a buffalo in the US and Canada, this large bovine is actually more closely related to yaks and cattle than to true buffalo — which animal?
Also nicknamed 'starflower,' this Mediterranean annual herb yields seed oil despite containing small amounts of toxic alkaloids — which plant?
Borage: Species of flowering plant in the family Boraginaceae.
One of the largest snake species on Earth, this Southeast Asian native became invasive in Florida after escaping the pet trade — which snake is this?
Burmese python: Species of large, nonvenomous snake.
Produced by chili peppers likely to deter hungry mammals, this hydrophobic compound is what gives them their burning, pungent kick — what is it?
Capsaicin: Pungent chemical compound in chili peppers. It is a potent irritant for mammals for which it produces a sensation of burning in any tissue with which it comes into contact.

This biological process splits a parent into two daughters, either producing genetically identical copies via mitosis or reducing chromosome number by half via meiosis to form gametes. What process is it?
Cell division: Biological process. Cell division usually occurs as part of a larger cell cycle in which the cell grows and replicates its chromosome(s) before dividing.
Known for a bitter metallic aftertaste that gets worse if you rinse with water, this antiseptic is used before surgery and to prevent dental plaque — what is it?
Chlorhexidine: Disinfectant and antiseptic. Chlorhexidine is a disinfectant and antiseptic which is used for skin disinfection before surgery and to disinfect surgical instruments.

First discovered as an atypical antipsychotic, this medication is reserved for schizophrenia patients who haven't responded to two other drugs, and is also used for psychosis linked to Parkinson's disease — what is it?
Clozapine: Atypical antipsychotic medication. Clozapine, sold under the brand name Clozaril among others, is a psychiatric medication and was the first atypical antipsychotic to be discovered.
These wind-pollinated, cone-bearing evergreens dominated Earth's landscapes throughout the Mesozoic before flowering plants took over — what group of plants is this?
Conifer: Group of seed plants. As of 2025, 94 conifer species are listed as endangered and 30 as critically endangered.
Their Latin name means 'those with shells,' and this mostly aquatic group includes crabs, lobsters, krill, barnacles, and mantis shrimp — what are they?
Named for a 19th-century British mathematician, this pair of logic rules shows how 'and' and 'or' swap places under negation — what are they called?
De Morgan's laws: Pair of logical equivalences.

Sudden lower-abdominal pain, sometimes a 'smoldering' slow burn over days — and the trouble is little abnormal pouches inflaming in the wall of your large intestine. What gastrointestinal disease is this?
Diverticulitis: Digestive disease of the large intestine. People may experience a single attack, repeated attacks, or ongoing "smoldering" diverticulitis.
Also known as dropsy, this medical condition involves fluid buildup in body tissue, often causing swelling in the legs or arms — what is it?
Edema: Accumulation of excess fluid in tissue.
A sympathomimetic stimulant often used to keep blood pressure up during anesthesia, this drug has also been tried for asthma, narcolepsy, and obesity — what is it?

Ranging from Northern Europe through Siberia to the Himalayas, this medium-sized wild cat is one of only four living species in its genus and can be found at elevations up to 5,500 meters — what animal is this?
Eurasian lynx: Species of medium-sized cat native to Eurasia.
This number-theory rule holds that if p is prime, then for any integer a, the value a to the power p minus a is always a multiple of p — which rule is this?

Fermat's little theorem: A prime p divides a^p–a for any integer a. Fermat's little theorem is the basis for the Fermat primality test and is one of the fundamental results of elementary number theory.
Marked by physical traits such as a long face, large ears, and unusually flexible fingers, this inherited neurodevelopmental disorder stems from a repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene — which condition?
Fragile X syndrome: X-linked dominant genetic disorder.
Found on every continent except Antarctica, these lizards are unusual for making vocal chirps and clicks, and most lack eyelids, relying on a transparent membrane instead — what are they?
Gecko: Lizards belonging to the suborder Gekkota.
Occurring in the cytosol, this ten-step metabolic pathway breaks glucose down into pyruvate while generating ATP and NADH — what process is it?
Glycolysis: Series of interconnected biochemical reactions.
After a record 43 years as crown prince, this Swedish monarch approved constitutional reforms stripping the crown of its remaining political powers shortly before his 1973 death. Who was he?
Gustaf VI Adolf: King of Sweden from 1950 to 1973.
In their normal state these vascular cushions in the anal canal actually help with stool control; only when swollen or inflamed do they become the condition also known as piles — what is it?
Hemorrhoid: Vascular structures in the anal canal. The signs and symptoms of hemorrhoids depend on the type present.
Damage to the sympathetic trunk nerves produces this trio of symptoms on one side of the face — a constricted pupil, a droopy eyelid, and reduced sweating — what is this condition called?
Horner's syndrome: Facial disorder due to damage of the sympathetic nerves.
Marked in its severe stage by hallucinations and paradoxical undressing, which condition is defined as a body core temperature below 35 degrees Celsius?
Hypothermia: Human body core temperature below 35 °C (95 °F)
Known historically as green vitriol or copperas, this blue-green heptahydrate salt is used to treat anemia and forms a paramagnetic octahedral complex in water — which compound?
Iron(II) sulfate: Chemical compound. Iron(II) sulfate or ferrous sulfate (British English: sulphate instead of sulfate) denotes a range of salts with the formula FeSO4·xH2O.
Son of Taiwanese immigrants, this engineer launched the world's most valuable company from a Denny's restaurant in 1993 after earning a Stanford master's degree — who is he?
Jensen Huang: Taiwanese and American businessman (born 1963)
Sometimes grown just for looks, this cabbage relative's leaves can be bumpy, curly, or flat, in colors from purple to green — what leafy vegetable is it?
Kale: Form of cabbage with green or purple leaves.
Born of Peranakan Chinese cuisine, this spicy Southeast Asian noodle dish is often served in a rich coconut-curry soup soured with tamarind — what is it?
Laksa: Spicy noodle dish from Southeast Asia.
This fibrous connective tissue links bone to bone in every one of the 30,000 known amniote species, and in birds it even anchors flight feathers to bone — what is it?

This Canadian physicist worked on the Manhattan Project determining critical mass values for uranium and plutonium, and in 1946 was fatally exposed to radiation in a lab accident at Los Alamos — who is he?
Louis Slotin: Canadian physicist and chemist (1910–1946)
Nicknamed sea cows, these slow-moving herbivorous mammals graze on more than 60 kinds of aquatic plants in the Caribbean, the Amazon basin, and West Africa — what are they?
Manatee: Genus of mammals. The main causes of death for manatees are human-related issues, such as habitat destruction and human objects.
Diagnosis, prognosis, prevention, treatment and palliation of injury and disease — drawing on biomedical science, genetics and technology — define this science and practice. What is it?

Medicine: Diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of illness. Medicine encompasses a variety of health care practices which evolved to maintain and restore health through the prevention and treatment of illness and infection.
Son of a U.S. vice president, this young art collector vanished in 1961 during an expedition into New Guinea's Asmat region, with some accounts claiming he was killed by local tribesmen — who was he?
Michael Rockefeller: American anthropologist and art collector (1938–1961)
Originally a dry-season staple for ǃKung hunter-gatherers, this tropical vine in the Cucurbitaceae family produces an intensely bitter edible fruit widely used across Asian cuisine — what is it?
Momordica charantia: Species of plant in the gourd family.
Found in cardiac and skeletal muscle and distantly related to hemoglobin, high levels of this oxygen-storing protein let diving whales and seals hold their breath longer — which protein?
Also known as black cumin or kalonji, this flowering plant native to the Levant and Iran is used across the world as a culinary spice — which species is it?
Nigella sativa: Species of flowering plant in the buttercup family.
This physics principle states that current through a conductor is directly proportional to the voltage across it, expressed as V equals I times R — what's it called?
Ohm's law: Law of electrical current and voltage. Ohm's law states that the electric current through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage across the two points.
Sold in extended-release form under the brand name OxyContin, this highly addictive semi-synthetic opioid treats moderate to severe pain and brings relief within about fifteen minutes. What is it?
Oxycodone: Opioid medication. It is usually taken orally, and is available in immediate-release and controlled-release formulations.
Named Pisum sativum by Carl Linnaeus in 1753, this pulse crop's pods are botanically a fruit containing seeds with green or yellow cotyledons — what vegetable is it?
Pea: Species of plant with edible seeds.
Found naturally in mammals' milk and a direct precursor to phenethylamine, this is one of nine amino acids your body can't make, so you eat it in meat, eggs, and legumes — which one?

There are exactly five of these convex regular polyhedra — tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron — named for the philosopher who linked them to the classical elements. What are they called?
Platonic solid: Any of the five regular polyhedra. In geometry, a Platonic solid is a convex, regular polyhedron in three-dimensional Euclidean space.

A trained engineer by profession, this royal consort married King Mohammed VI in 2002, becoming the first publicly acknowledged wife of a reigning monarch there to hold an official title, before their discreet 2018 divorce. Who is she?
Princess Lalla Salma of Morocco: Moroccan royal (born 1978)
Imagine a benzene ring with one CH swapped for a nitrogen atom: the result is this flammable, fish-smelling liquid once distilled from coal tar and now made at 20,000 tons a year — what is it?

This Canadian-American inventor pulled off the first transmission of speech by radio in 1900 and the first two-way radiotelegraphy across the Atlantic in 1906, racking up hundreds of patents — seven granted after his death. Who was this AM-radio pioneer?
Reginald Fessenden: Canadian-American electrical engineer and inventor (1866–1932)
Commonly called the dog rose, this variable climbing wild plant is native to Europe, northwest Africa, and western Asia — which species?
Also known as mucopolysaccharidosis type III, this rare genetic disorder is caused by the body's inability to break down certain sugar molecules called glycosaminoglycans — what is it called?

Sanfilippo syndrome: Rare metabolism disorder. Sanfilippo syndrome, also known as mucopolysaccharidosis type III (MPS III), is a rare lifelong genetic disease that mainly affects the brain and spinal cord.
Born in Moscow and brought to the US at age six, this computer scientist co-founded Google with Larry Page and served as president of its parent company until 2019 — who is he?
Sometimes triggered just by stepping into bright sunlight, a quirk called the photic reflex, this involuntary, explosive expulsion of air clears irritants from the nose and mouth. What is it?
Sneeze: Semi-autonomous, convulsive expulsion of air from the lungs through the nose and mouth.
